title: Strong connections share more partners in four fly and mouse connectomes after neuron and region controls; cell-type pairs give most fly clustering, and mouse shared partners do not track tuning
abstract: Question: Lynn et al. (Nature Physics 2024) state that Hebbian growth explains why strong connections are clustered in connectomes. We tested this claim in four connectomes they did not fully use: FlyWire FAFB 783 (138,639 neurons), hemibrain v1.2, MANC v1.0 nerve cord and MICrONS minnie65 v1300 mouse visual cortex (edges from 2,064 proofread axons). Method: for each neuron pair we counted shared partners (triangles) and compared strong and weak pairs with nested controls: two-way neuron fixed effects, region overlap or soma distance, and cell-type-pair fixed effects; we also made Lynn-style threshold curves with free, neuron-strength-stratified and cell-type-pair weight permutations, and a calibrated mixing null. In MICrONS we linked shared partners to response similarity from Ding et al. 2025. Results: in all four connectomes, global clustering among strong pairs stays far above free permutations while density falls by 2.4 to 2.8 orders of magnitude, so the descriptive claim replicates. Neuron-strength nulls reproduce only 0% to 20% of the excess at the strongest thresholds. In fly, cell-type-pair permutations reproduce a median 56% to 83% of the excess beyond retained pairs; in mouse, with coarse types, 3%. Per doubling of synapse count, log(1 + shared partners) rises by 0.19 to 0.54 without controls and by 0.041 to 0.131 after all controls (node-jackknife SE 0.0005 to 0.003); 20% to 45% of the raw slope stays in fly and about 10% in mouse. In MICrONS, shared partners did not predict response similarity after neuron, distance and area-layer controls in 8 of 9 tests (connected, proximity-only and same-region pairs), and response similarity did not change the synapse-count slope of shared partners (0.058 to 0.057). Conclusion: strong connections are clustered, but in fly this is mostly a cell-type property, in mouse mostly neuron identity and distance, and we found no link to co-tuning. A small within-type link stays. Limitations: region and distance bins are proxies for arbor contact; type labels partly use connectivity; one mouse and few multi-synapse pairs limit the function test.

display.caption: Global clustering (transitivity) of pairs above a synapse threshold versus density, in four connectomes. Blue: measured. Grey: weights permuted freely on the base graph. Orange: weights permuted inside strata of the neuron-only prediction. Green: weights permuted inside cell-type-pair blocks. Dotted: clustering equal to density.
Edge-level slope of log(1 + shared partners) (left) and edge clustering (right) per doubling of synapse count, with nested controls. Error bars: 95% node-group jackknife.

MICrONS: raw response similarity and soma distance by shared-partner bin for connected and unconnected pairs (left, middle), and standardized effects of shared partners on three similarity measures after neuron, distance and area-layer controls (right, 95% jackknife intervals).
